blocks.prompt: The Storm That Touches the Ground
blocks.text: A tornado is a tube of spinning air. It hangs down from a thunderstorm. To be a real tornado, it has to touch the cloud and the ground at the same time. If it does not touch the ground, it is only a funnel. You can see a tornado because it picks up dust and dirt. The air by itself is invisible. Most tornadoes are small. Most of them are gone in a few minutes. But the wind inside can lift a roof off a house. When a warning comes, your family goes to the lowest room. You stay away from windows. You wait until it passes.

answers: the cloud and the ground at the same time
a funnel
it picks up dust and dirt
to the lowest room, away from windows

blocks.prompt: How a Storm Grows a Tail
blocks.text: Warm wet air near the ground wants to rise. Cool dry air sits above it. When the warm air pushes up fast, it builds a thunderstorm that can stand taller than a mountain. Now add wind. Near the ground the wind blows one way, and high up it blows a different way at a different speed. That difference makes the air between them roll over, like a log spinning on its side. The rising air in the storm grabs that rolling log and tips it upright. Now the whole middle of the storm is turning. If that spinning column stretches down out of the cloud and touches the ground, it is a tornado. If it hangs in the air and never reaches the ground, it is only a funnel cloud. You do not see the wind. Wind is invisible. You see the tornado because the spinning air pulls water droplets out of the sky and rips dirt off the field. What you are watching is the mess it carries.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.

answers: warm wet air near the ground and cool dry air above it
it tips it upright, so the middle of the storm turns
touch the ground
(inference: the difference between the two winds is what starts the air rolling)

4.title: The Storm That Touches the Ground
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Storm That Touches the Ground

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Most strong ones come from supercells
The spinning core is a mesocyclone
Nothing survives inside to measure it
Ted Fujita built his scale in 1971
EF0 peels shingles, EF5 clears a house
The rating is given after the storm is gone

blocks.prompt: Measuring a Wind Nobody Can Reach
blocks.text: Most strong tornadoes are born inside a supercell, a thunderstorm with a rotating engine at its heart. Meteorologists call that spinning core a mesocyclone. It can be several miles wide, and it turns slowly enough that a person standing underneath might not notice it at all. The tornado itself is the narrow part. As the mesocyclone tightens, it spins faster, the way a skater spins faster by pulling her arms in. A column of air drops out of the cloud base, and if it reaches the ground, the storm has a tornado. Here is the problem for scientists. You cannot put a thermometer or a wind gauge inside a tornado. Anything you leave in its path is likely to be destroyed or carried away. So for years there was no good way to say how strong one was. Ted Fujita solved it backward. In 1971 he built a scale that measures the damage instead of the wind, then works out the wind speed from what the storm broke. The United States now uses an updated version called the Enhanced Fujita scale. EF0 peels shingles off a roof. EF5 sweeps a well built house clean off its foundation. The rating is always assigned after the tornado is gone, by people walking through the wreckage. That is why a tornado on the news has no number at first. The number comes later, once someone has seen what it did.

blocks.prompt: The Country That Gets the Most
blocks.text: The United States records roughly 1,200 tornadoes a year, more than any other country on Earth. That is not bad luck. It is geography. Look at a map. The Rocky Mountains run down the west of the continent, and the Gulf of Mexico sits open at the south. Warm, wet air streams north off the Gulf and slides along near the ground. Cool, dry air comes over the Rockies and rides above it. Nothing blocks them from meeting. There is no mountain range running east to west across the middle of the country to keep the two apart. So they collide over the Great Plains, one air mass stacked on top of the other, and the atmosphere becomes unstable in exactly the way a supercell needs. For decades this stretch of the Plains has been nicknamed Tornado Alley. The nickname is useful and slightly misleading. Tornadoes have been recorded in every state, and researchers tracking recent decades have noted that damaging tornadoes are becoming more common further east, across states like Mississippi, Alabama, and Tennessee. Those states are more wooded, more densely populated, and get more of their tornadoes at night, which makes them harder to see coming and harder to escape. The American answer to all this is warning. Doppler radar does not show a tornado directly. It shows the wind moving toward and away from the radar, and where those two sit side by side, the storm is rotating. Forecasters watching that signature can issue a warning before anything touches the ground. A tornado watch means the ingredients are present and you should pay attention. A tornado warning means one has been sighted or shows on radar, and you should already be moving. The average warning now arrives about thirteen minutes ahead. Thirteen minutes is not long. It is enough to reach a basement, and that is the whole point of it.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Storm That Touches the Ground

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Tornadogenesis is still an open question
Wind shear rolls the air, the updraft tilts it
Fastest wind on record: about 300 mph, Oklahoma, 1999
Widest on record: 2.6 miles, El Reno, 2013
Deadliest US tornado: Tri-State, 1925, 695 dead

blocks.prompt: The Question Nobody Has Answered Yet
blocks.text: Here is something strange about tornadoes. We can photograph them, fly aircraft around them, and hit them with research radar that samples the wind every few seconds. We can forecast the conditions that produce them days in advance. And we still cannot reliably say why one supercell drops a tornado while the supercell twenty miles behind it, sitting in what looks like identical air, never does. The broad picture is settled. A supercell is a thunderstorm with a rotating updraft called a mesocyclone, born when wind shear, meaning wind that changes speed and direction with height, sets a horizontal tube of air rolling, and the storm's updraft tilts that tube upright. Stretch a spinning column and it spins faster, the same reason a skater accelerates when she pulls in her arms. What remains unsettled is the last step down. Tornadoes appear to require rotation gathered near the ground, not just borrowed from above, and the processes that concentrate it there involve the storm's cold downdraft, its outflow, and temperature differences of only a few degrees. Get those wrong and the storm produces nothing. The measurement problem makes this worse. Instruments placed in a tornado's path are usually destroyed, and the few that survive sample one point for a few seconds. So meteorologists went mobile. The VORTEX projects sent fleets of trucks, radars, and weather balloons chasing storms across the Plains, and Doppler on Wheels radar took the fastest wind ever recorded on Earth: about 300 miles per hour, near Bridge Creek, Oklahoma, on May 3, 1999. That reading came from radar aimed at the tornado from a safe distance, not from a gauge inside it. Nothing survives inside it. Rating tornadoes has the same problem, which is why the Enhanced Fujita scale still works backward from damage rather than forward from wind. It is an ingenious workaround, and it has a real weakness. A violent tornado that crosses empty pasture breaks nothing worth rating, so it may be logged as weak. The scale measures what a storm hit, not what it was. The extremes are worth knowing. The widest tornado ever measured was 2.6 miles across, near El Reno, Oklahoma, in 2013. The deadliest in American history was the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925, which ran roughly 219 miles across Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana and killed 695 people, in an era with no radar, no watches, and no warnings. Compare that to now. The average tornado warning arrives about thirteen minutes before the storm, and those thirteen minutes are the difference between 1925 and today. So the honest summary is this. We know what tornadoes are made of. We know roughly where and when to expect them. We can warn you. We cannot yet tell you which storm.
